title: Your pregnancy bill is changing in January. Here is what it means.
summary: Starting January 1, 2027, the way pregnancy care is billed to insurance changes across the country. The care does not change. The paperwork behind it does. Here is what patients are likely to notice, in plain language, plus a short script for the front desk staff who are about to start getting these questions.
body_markdown:
This page has two parts. The first is written for patients and is meant to be shared or handed out. The second is for front desk and billing staff.


## For patients


### Something is changing, and it is not your care


Starting January 1, 2027, the way pregnancy care gets billed to insurance is changing across the country.


Nothing about your actual care changes. Same visits, same doctor or midwife, same delivery. What changes is the paperwork behind it.


### What was happening before


Until now, most pregnancy care was billed as one package. Your prenatal visits, your delivery and your check-up afterward were bundled into a single charge, usually submitted after you delivered.


That is why many people got almost no bills during pregnancy and then one large one at the end.


### What is changing


From January, that package comes apart. Your prenatal visits, your delivery and your postpartum care get billed separately, closer to when each one happens.


### What you are likely to notice


**More pieces of mail, spread over more months.** You may get a statement or an explanation of benefits after individual visits rather than one at the end. More envelopes does not automatically mean more money.


**Your estimate may be harder to pin down.** Insurance companies are still publishing their 2027 rates. If your practice cannot give you an exact number yet, that is honest rather than evasive.


**If you prepay, ask how your plan is being handled.** Some practices collect for pregnancy care up front or in monthly installments. Those arrangements were built around the old bundled charge, and each practice is adjusting them differently.


**If you are due early in 2027, your care will straddle the change.** Some of your visits happened under the old rules and some will fall under the new ones. That is expected. It is not a mistake, and it does not mean you are being billed twice.


### Will you pay more?


Honestly, it depends on your plan, and nobody can give you a universal answer yet.


Here is what we can tell you. We read insurer policies on this full time, and most of the notices we have read either say nothing about what patients pay, or say it should not change. Several state specifically that routine prenatal visits remain preventive care with no additional cost to you.


That is not a guarantee for your plan. It is a reason not to panic.


### What to do


**Ask your practice how they are handling the transition.** They have been planning for this.


**If you prepaid or set up a payment plan, ask what happens to it.**


**Keep your statements.** If something looks duplicated or wrong, it is much easier to sort out with the paperwork in front of you.


**Call the number on your insurance card** for questions about your own coverage. Your practice can tell you how they bill. Only your insurer can tell you what your plan pays.


## For the front desk


Short answers to the questions you are about to start getting. Say the quiet version, not the coding version.


**"Why am I getting more bills than my sister did?"**
The way pregnancy care is billed changed on January 1. It used to be one bundled charge at the end. Now each part is billed as it happens. More statements, not automatically more cost.


**"Am I paying more than I would have last year?"**
It depends on your plan. Most insurers have said patient costs for routine prenatal care should not change, but final 2027 rates are still being published. We can tell you what we bill. Your insurer is the one who can tell you what you owe.


**"Can you give me an estimate?"**
We can give you one based on what we know today, with the caveat that the rates are still being finalized.


**"I already paid for my whole pregnancy up front. What now?"**
Route to billing. Do not improvise an answer. Prepayment and installment arrangements were built around the old bundled charge and each practice is unwinding them differently.


**"My insurance says they have no record of my pregnancy charges."**
Likely a timing issue. Charges now go out closer to each visit rather than in one batch after delivery, so the two sides can be out of step for a while.


**"Did my doctor change something?"**
No. The change came from the national coding standards, not from this practice. Nothing about the care is different.


### Two rules for staff


**Do not guess at a number.** "I don't want to give you a figure I'd have to take back" is a better answer than a wrong one.


**Do not blame the insurer in front of the patient.** It is a scheduled national change, not a dispute.


## Where this comes from


We track over 3000 health plans and read their maternity policies as they publish. Every provider organization we could find that delivers babies has a public page listing its payers, what each has published, the effective date, and a link to the source. Free, no form, no sign-up.


[The 2027 Maternity Resource Center](https://www.substrateai.com/payers/2027-substrate-maternity-resource-center)
